Psychodynamic milieu-therapy and changes in personality – what is the connection?1

Tine Heede , Hanne Runge , Ole Storebø , Eva Rowley and Kim Hansen

Kim Hansen

Kim Hansen  

Milieu-therapy, effect evaluation, Rorschach, children, TAT

This article refers to the results of a prospective effect evaluation study of three psychodynamic milieu-therapeutic institutions for children, which included cognitive and projective testing. After introducing milieu-therapy and explaining its roots in psychoanalytic and developmental thinking, the specific results of the research evaluation are outlined. It is found that environmental therapy is very efficient on the level of ego-functioning, but concern is expressed in regards to the relational abilities of the children. These findings are discussed in relation to the practical, organisational and theoretical principles of the actual treatment in order to find ways to improve our understanding of how milieu-therapy works and how it can be improved. Finally, we discuss the ways in which recent theoretical and empiric research emphasising the importance of the affect regulation and mentalisation can contribute to the psychoanalytic theories in the milieu-therapy.

Patients' experiences of self-disclosure in psychotherapy: the effects of gender and gender role identification

Dailey Pattee & Barry A. Farber

Psychotherapy Research, Taylor and Francis, May 2008, Volume 18 (3): 306–15

This study examined the effects of gender and gender role identification on 223 patients' experiences of self-disclosure in psychotherapy. Factor analysis of the Disclosure-to-Therapist Inventory-IV revealed two dimensions: a distress factor, reflecting the perceived difficulty and the anticipated impact of disclosures on the therapist, and an openness factor, reflecting the extent and perceived importance of disclosures and the interpersonal connection experienced during them. Female patients working with female therapists experienced greater distress in disclosure than male patients working with female therapists; in addition, patients with more flexible gender role identifications (i.e., androgynous) experienced greater openness than those with more traditional gender identifications. Findings suggest a need for greater discussion in therapy of the effects of gender on disclosure.

Tomboys: meanings, marginalization, and misunderstandings

Joanne M. Hall

Issues in Mental Health Nursing, Taylor and Francis, June 2008, Volume 29 (6): 555–65

Girls who act like boys are called ‘tomboys’. This is an exploration using feminist guiding principles, about what ‘tomboyism’ means to children and how adults around them construct it. The purpose is to examine tomboyism from literary, linguistic, historical and cultural perspectives. The exploration includes a review of selected scientific sources, children's and some adult literature, and conversations with adult women who recall their tomboyism from youth and how it now affects them as adults.

Clinical commentary by Debbie Hindle, a child and adolescent psychotherapist working in Glasgow and organizing tutor of the clinical training at the Scottish Institute of Human Relations

From a research perspective

In the background to the clinical material, the therapist identifies these sessions as a ‘turning point in the work’. So I thought I would begin by considering the research on turning point sessions in child psychotherapy before thinking about the complex issues that this young child and her therapist were grappling with together.

Carlberg (1997: 331) defined a turning point session as

a session where the therapist notices that something qualitatively new may be identified concerning the behaviour of the child or the child's way of showing his/ her inner world, or where something new enters the interplay between the child and the therapist.

Carlberg's small qualitative study is fascinating to read, as he was able to identify common features, as well as a range of themes that emerged in the cases reported over a two-year period.

In relation to the clinical material described in this commentary, I was struck by the directness of Grace's communication to her therapist, and the way in which they came together to create a narrative, with the therapist giving voice to Grace's feelings. These moments – also captured by Grace's words and actions – seem to exemplify what Carlberg (1997: 345) described as a key principle behind these kinds of changes – ‘a moment of emotional meeting underlying the turning point’. That is, it is in the context of the relationship and the emotional quality of the interplay between child and therapist that seems to pave the way for such changes.

Carlberg (1997: 342) also noted that ‘there is often an extended significant process preceding the turning’. In the therapist's background information, we hear that in the initial period of the therapy, Grace was ‘often silent or spoke only in whispers … or was hidden in corners of the room or under the blanket’. She describes how ‘sessions appeared more like infant observations, with only fragments of play discernible’. I found myself wondering if the therapist's observation skills, her capacity to accurately and attentively observe, as evidenced by her detailed recordings of the sessions given, provided an important context for the work we see emerging in these sessions.

Clinical commentary

Graham Music

Graham Music

Graham Music  

The following clinical commentary continues the theme of discussing work done by child psychotherapists in a variety of contexts by describing psychotherapeutic work undertaken in a school setting. The discussions that follow are able to describe what is ordinarily psychotherapeutic about such work, as well as the ways in which technique and thinking about practice might or might not be altered by work in settings where direct clinical work is less usual.

Clinical material

Background

Sam is a 14-year-old boy, whom I have been seeing for once-weekly psychotherapy at his school. I have been working with him for two and a half years.

Sam lived with his mother, mother's partner and younger half-brother until he was six years old. Sam's mother and her partner were drug-addicted alcoholics, who were involved in domestic violence towards each other and the children, especially Sam. Sam felt responsible for his sibling and tried to protect him. Sam would rarely attend school, often went hungry and was frequently living in fear for his and his mother's life. Sam was eventually removed from his mother's care, to live with his father with whom he had had intermittent contact throughout his life. Sam currently lives with his father, father's partner and their three-year-old son. This home provides him with stability and basic care, but falls far short of providing for him emotionally. Sam has no contact with his maternal half-brother. Sam has intermittent contact with his mother, who continues to abuse alcohol and he constantly worries about her.

He was referred by a psychotherapist from the specialist unit he had previously attended. This was due to severe emotional and behavioural difficulties that inhibited him accessing the academic and social curriculum. There had been some anxiety from the referrer that he was borderline psychotic. He was seen in school as his father would not engage with mental health professionals and would not have brought him to a clinic.

Sam engaged very well in therapy and attended well until some recent involvement of Social Services. Sam continues to have difficulties managing school. His behaviour has gradually improved, as has his academic work, although he is still underachieving and remains socially isolated. However, he has recently started a part-time college placement doing an Arts and Media course and is doing very well there.

Clinical commentary by Emil Jackson, consultant child & adolescent psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic and Brent Centre for Young People

This clinical extract raises many interesting and important issues. In this brief commentary, I will focus on three important themes, namely: the impact of the setting of this work, the case material itself and the importance of maintaining the therapeutic setting in our mind.

Child psychotherapy in schools

The school-based context for this work raises a number of immediate questions. What is it like for us to apply our thinking and work within a school setting? How do we need to adapt the way we work, think and take up our role? How do we experience and manage our relationships with teachers and parents? What is (or isn't) different about this from work within a more ‘ordinary’ outpatient CAMHS setting? Is ‘child psychotherapy’ really possible within a school?

In principle – most of us would agree that there is a need for child psychotherapy to extend itself into community-based settings such as schools to ensure that we reach those children and young people who would never otherwise make it to an outpatient setting.

Claudia McLoughlin

Claudia McLoughlin  

Clinical commentary by Claudia McLoughlin, child & adolescent psychotherapist, Islington Community CAMHS

Reflections on the background description

I was asked to comment on this session because it takes place in the school setting, which is familiar to me through my work over the past six years for the Islington CAMHS in Education Service. In the context of my own attempts at working therapeutically in both mainstream schools and units for excluded pupils, the first sentence in the ‘Background’ paragraph of the material provided immediately interested me: here was a therapist who sounded quite confident that what she was providing to her patient in this setting was once weekly psychotherapy. In my own Service, those of us who are psychotherapists have been debating for a long time whether what we offer in the educational setting, even when it is long-term, once-weekly individual work, could ever be called psychoanalytic psychotherapy, due to the many adaptations in technique necessitated by not being in a clinic environment and culture. We have come to the conclusion that at times we are able to offer something akin to what Otto Kernberg (2004) called ‘supportive psychotherapy’, and after reading to the end of the clinical session presented, it seemed to me that it was very much that particular form of psychotherapy this therapist was offering to Sam. I will come back to this perhaps controversial point later.

Sam's life history and present living circumstances sounded sadly familiar in the context of my Pupil Referral Unit (PRU) work. I found myself impressed that he had managed to reintegrate relatively successfully back into a mainstream school, given the level of neglect, physical and emotional abuse he had suffered during his early years, and the statement that his emotional needs were still not being met at home by his father and his new family. He sounded like a resilient and resourceful young person to me, who was able to make the best of whatever help was being offered to him. I found myself thinking that given this, his protectiveness of his younger half brother in the past and his consistently caring attitude towards his mother over the years, there also must have been a more positive, benign aspect to the early attachment relationship between Sam and his mother on a profound level. I would be curious to know the details of his early history, and the history of his parents' relationship. I would also have liked to hear more about Sam's previous therapist's concerns about Sam being ‘borderline psychotic’, which sounded like quite a shocking pronouncement about a then 12-year-old child. Using a Kleinian framework of understanding, my guess would be that the therapist meant that Sam was often in a persecuted, paranoid–schizoid rather than depressive state of mind and indeed there was evidence in the account that followed that this was still the case. He was described as ‘still socially isolated’, and he had stopped coming to his therapy sessions in the wake of a renewed Social Services Assessment of his family situation.

Clinical commentary by David Trevatt, Clinical Manager of ‘Hear and Now’ Adolescent Counselling Service, Redbridge and Manager of Open Door's Parenting Teenagers Project, Haringey

I am interested in this case as an example of therapeutic work undertaken in school. Although the school setting is not particularly apparent in the case material, I think it is probably very significant when considering the nature of the case and how the work has been managed by the therapist, with all the institutional dynamics that schools present.

It is clear that Sam has had a very deprived and difficult early life. Central to his experience is that he has experienced the failure of a parent being able to offer him adequate and permanent care. Perhaps his experience was of having a mother with drug and alcohol problems, which can often result in far from consistent parenting, and with the additional feature of being physically present and emotionally absent or unavailable.

It is difficult to know the extent and the detail of his experience of neglect and physical threat, and also to know how he managed himself through that time. It seems clear that in the session he becomes very much in touch with images and feelings of his poor care and living conditions.

Issues of ‘race’ in psychoanalytic psychotherapy: whose problem is it anyway?

Helen Morgan

British Journal of Psychotherapy, Wiley-Blackwell, December 2007, Volume 24 (1): 34–49

The author argues in this paper that, because of racism, there is an asymmetrical power relationship between black and white which saturates all aspects of society. Whilst this dynamic also permeates psychoanalytic training organizations the problem is frequently ignored or denied. This colour-blind position fails to see or acknowledge difference and hence the white individual is able to avoid the shame involved in owning any racist thought. For the black trainee an important aspect of their identity and experience is not allowed expression, making the training experience a difficult one. However, the paper argues that the inability to acknowledge and think about racism has implications, not only for potential black applicants and patients, but also for the professional organizations and their predominantly white members as this cordial form of racism prevents thought and does damage to both white and black.

Process and outcome of therapy in ethnically similar and dissimilar therapeutic dyads

Farkhondeh Farsimadan, Riccardo Draghi-Lorenz & Jason Ellis

Psychotherapy Research, Routledge, September 2007, Volume 17 (5): 567–75

This study examined the effects of ethnic matching on two process variables – working alliance and perceived therapist credibility – and therapy outcome in 100 ethnic minority clients evenly split between matched and nonmatched therapeutic dyads. All clients and therapists belonged to ethnic minorities in London (South Asian, Black African, Black Caribbean, and Middle Eastern). Clients in the matched dyads had expressed a preference for matching. Outcome and process variables were all significantly better in matched than in nonmatched dyads, and the process variables mediated the relationship between ethnic matching and outcome. Age, gender, and length of therapy did not predict outcome or process. The validity of these results is discussed, and implications for further research, practice, and training are briefly considered.

Child psychotherapy and research

Debbie Hindle

Debbie Hindle

Debbie Hindle  

Child psychotherapy and research, edited by Nick Midgley, Jan Anderson, Eve Grainger, Tanja Nesic-Vuckovic and Cathy Urwin, London, Routledge, 2009, 248 pp., £22.99

This is a welcome and truly timely publication at a point when we need to arm ourselves with the evidence that has accumulated and to be able to communicate our findings. This book may stand as a milestone in the profession, marking a new era in relation to how we think about and approach research in child psychotherapy. Increasingly, in any service or private practice, we need to hold what I have come to call a ‘research state of mind’ in which audit, single case studies, involvement in service-based studies or larger profession-based studies become a mainstream activity. This contributes to the validity of what we know, what we do and may raise further questions for exploration. It is after all, this openness, curiosity and sense of discovery that is embedded in psychoanalytic thinking and clinical work.

The book opens with an eloquent Preface by Peter Hobson, in which he succinctly outlines the potential tensions between the aims of research and the special conditions, practice and power of child psychotherapy. He states (p. xvi):

What research needs to offer – and what this book offers – are creative ways of capturing relevant aspects of the things that child psychotherapists do and observe, and/or what child psychotherapists have discerned to be important in and beyond the consulting room, in such a way as to make these amenable to public awareness and subject to scientific evaluation.

What is helpful about the book is that it is so clearly structured, gathering together seminal papers which reflect different types of research that have taken place, delineating different methodologies used and introducing us to the diversity of research that has developed in the field.

The Introduction describes the contemporary context of child psychotherapy and the challenges we all face. The editors themselves state that the book supports ‘a pluralistic and pragmatic research agenda’ (p. 9). That is, it does not set out to define a research agenda, but gives voice to a complex and evolving field where different methodologies and foci of study have grown up (largely independently). What is conveyed is the ‘commitment to the importance of research in raising public awareness of child psychotherapy's field of practice, the evidence for its effectiveness and its potential contribution to knowledge’ (p. 10).

Francesco Bisagni, a psychiatrist, was trained as a Jungian analyst at the Centro Italiano di Psicologia Analitica (CIPA). He completed his training as a child and adolescent psychotherapist according to the Tavistock model at the Associazione Italiana di Psicoterapia Psicoanalitica Infantile (AIPPI), of which he was a full member from 1998 until 2007. He is presently a full member and training analyst at CIPA – Centro Italiano di Psicologia Analitica (IAAP Member). He is a member of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis (NAAP) in the United States. He has taught for many years both in Italy and abroad and has had his works published in Italian as well as in international journals. He is in private practice as a psychoanalyst and child psychotherapist in Milan.

Vera Regina Jardim Ribeiro Marcondes Fonseca is a psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, working since 1981 with children with autistic disorders. She is a full member, supervisor and training analyst of the Brazilian Psychoanalytic Society of São Paulo. Her doctoral thesis was about a psychoanalytic and ethologic interdisciplinary approach to interpersonal relationships in autistic disorders. She is currently a post-doctoral researcher at the Institute of Psychology, Department of Experimental Psychology at the University of São Paulo, studying mother–infant interactions in postpartum depression. She is supported by FAPESP's research fund in São Paulo, Brazil.

Kim Gabriel Hansen is a specialist and supervisor in psychotherapy in Denmark. He works in private practice where he teaches and supervises psychological assessment and psychotherapy with adults and children. He has specialised in personality performance tests and research.

Tine Heede is chief psychologist at the Nebs Møllegård residential home for deprived and traumatised children in Denmark, and she is a specialist and supervisor in child psychology. She is Chair of the board of education in psychoanalytical psychotherapy with children and adolescents in the Danish Society of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, where she also teaches and supervises. She is currently finishing a randomised trial on psychodynamic group intervention with overweight children and their families at the Department of Paediatrics, Hillerød, Denmark.

Deborah Marks

Deborah Marks  

The anorexic mind

The anorexic mind, by Marilyn Lawrence, London, Karnac, 2008, 143 pp., £18.99, ISBN-10: 1855753839, ISBN-13: 978-1855753839

When Freud first discovered that his patient Emmy von N. was covertly disposing of her pudding by throwing it out of the window, his insistence that she eat and drink more was met by ‘open rebellion’ (Breuer and Freud, 1895: 81). His irritation with her intransigence is transparent. Many since have commented on the strong feelings that arise in the countertransference towards anorexic patients, whose pathology is characterised, Lawrence suggests, by the refusal to accept help. Some of the intense frustration and anxiety evoked are related to the fact that the condition carries the highest mortality rate in young women (90% of sufferers are female) of any psychiatric illness. It is therefore unsurprising that a burgeoning psychoanalytic literature seeks to enlarge our understanding of the anorexic mind.

Marilyn Lawrence writes on the basis of 30 years of experience of individual psychoanalytic work with anorexic patients as well as, importantly, of consulting to the staff of specialist eating disorder units. Recognising the increasingly multidisciplinary design of treatment in inpatient settings, her book is written with a broad professional audience in mind: ‘an approach that helps practitioners to find meaning in the illnesses of their patients is likely to be helpful to mental health workers from a range of different backgrounds’ (p. 1). The book is a volume in the Tavistock Clinic Series, which sets out to make accessible the clinical and theoretical work of this institution. It is thus firmly situated in the Kleinian tradition and aims to provide a concise and approachable overview rather than a detailed or innovative account. Lawrence highlights that members of this patient group are difficult to think about, not least because they have such difficulty in thinking about themselves, and the book provides tools for thinking that are accessible to those largely unfamiliar with a psychoanalytic framework as well to those who are.

Mother-to-infant and father-to-infant initial emotional involvement

Bárbara Figueiredo, Raquel Costa, Alexandra Pacheco & Alvaro Pais

Early Child Development and Care, July 2007, Volume 177 (5): 521–32

While infant attachment has been largely studied, parental attachment is still relatively unknown, especially when referred to fathers. However, it is mainly recognised that parents' emotional involvement with the newborn contributes to the quality of the interaction and the care they provide. The aim of this study was to study mother-to-infant and father-to-infant initial emotional involvement; namely, differences between mothers and fathers and changes in mother's emotions toward the neonate within the first days after delivery. The Bonding Scale, an extended Portuguese version of the ‘New Mother-to-Infant Bonding Scale’, was administered during the first two days after childbirth to a sample of 315 mothers and 141 fathers (n = 456), at the Júlio Dinis Maternity Hospital (Portugal). Most mothers and fathers show positive emotions and only a few of them showed negative emotions toward the infant. Maternal and paternal emotional involvement toward the newborn tend to be similar; nevertheless, fathers show less fear and better emotional involvement with the neonate, while mothers are sadder and show more emotions not related to bonding. During the first days following delivery, emotions not related to bonding, such as fear, seem to decrease in mothers.

An empirical examination of toddler development in inclusive childcare

Aubyn C. Stahmer & Cynthia Carter

Early Child Development and Care, May 2005, Volume 175 (4): 321–33

An increasing number of families are enrolling their children in out-of-home early childcare services. In addition, a growing number of community childcare programs are including children with developmental disabilities. While some studies have explored the effects of inclusion for preschool children with disabilities, there is little knowledge about the effects of inclusion for typically developing toddlers enrolled in such programs. We recently published a study examining parent perceptions of the benefits and limitations of their child's toddler program (inclusion or typical), which found that parents were satisfied with and saw many benefits to inclusion. In the current study, we expand on that research by examining the social, behavioural, communication and cognitive development of toddlers enrolled in the same inclusion program. Scores on standardized assessments were compared with norms for those assessments, and outcomes indicate excellent gains in cognitive and language development and no detrimental behavioural effects of inclusion.

The waiting room position of mother alongside Grace is reminiscent of how mothers with babies in special care units are often sitting alongside, not quite present in the relationship. The waiting room also highlights the timelessness and the relentless waiting so central to the experience of having a premature baby. ‘Like watching wet paint dry.’ The therapist's sense of Grace being swamped in her school uniform also evokes an image of a premature baby too small for clothes and not yet in her own body. The tone of the first session, the cat sounds and hooting owls also depict a preverbal scene, where Grace's experiences seem so primitive that she has no words for them. Grace spells out that the cat's needs are basic, those of comfort, food and sleep, a clear reference to the simple but essential requirements of a baby.

The development of the play with the cat taking charge seems important in that Grace is attempting to master a situation, whereas in fact her early infancy would have been an experience of feeling overwhelmed and never being in charge, constantly being administered to and at the mercy of professionals. There is a sense of Grace working out her own capacities to know and regulate her own body for the first time, when she speaks of the cat “It needs to be in charge of how much light and sound …” The imagery of the cat also recalls a horror of not having been the perfect human baby her family might have wished for but rather an undeveloped animal.

The arrival of another kitten and then many babies in the play enables the shadow of the original baby to be more fully explored. As if it is only with the arrival of a full term healthy babying that the trauma of the premature baby can be realised. It is striking that Grace is referred for her constipation difficulties at the time of her sister's birth. Grace is emotionally ‘clogged up’ with all these earlier experiences, as if only then can the undigested trauma and loss be examined. There is a definite sense in the material that the original baby feels that she has been replaced because she was not good enough. The “you go to a different home” represents in unconscious fantasy the idea that she wasn't the baby they wanted. Also it feels hopeful that the therapy is a possible new home, where there can be a second chance to become a member of this family and a sense of belonging facilitated. The therapist is interested and focussed on in getting to know her. The therapy is a place where Grace is looked at with interested eyes, rather than anxious, disappointed or persecuting eyes.

Susan Isaacs: a life freeing the minds of children

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves  

Susan Isaacs: a life freeing the minds of children

Susan Isaacs: a life freeing the minds of children, by Philip Graham, London, Karnac, 2009, 352 pp., £29.99

To most readers of this journal the name of Susan Isaacs will be remembered, if at all, in connection with a series of papers she wrote, or co-wrote, as part of the Kleinian contribution to the so-called ‘Controversial Discussions’ that dominated the proceedings of the British Psychoanalytic Society during the period of the Second World War. Child psychotherapists trained at the Tavistock Clinic will almost certainly have read her paper on ‘The nature and function of phantasy’ (Isaacs, 1948), widely regarded as the classic statement of the Kleinian position on the role of the infant's earliest mental processes, and their impact on the later development of the personality. What they will not have derived from it is much of an impression of the author herself, other than that she is clearly articulate, definite in her views, and categorical in her manner of expressing them. They would certainly get no inkling from it that she was the person described, in the words of her entry in the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, as ‘the greatest influence on British education in the twentieth century’ (Pines, 2004).

Isaacs was a woman not just of many parts, but of many personas. The enigma of her personality is compounded by the fact that within the disciplines of education, child psychology and psychoanalysis, where she was once such a dominant figure, her contributions are nowadays practically forgotten. So it is a mark of her historical significance, as well as of her contemporary relevance, that one of the present-day luminaries in child psychiatry and child welfare, Philip Graham, has chosen to write this very substantial biography about her. In doing so, he has both amplified and moderated the earlier, rather hagiographic account of Susan Isaacs written by her former pupil, and later successor as Head of the Department of Child Development at the Institute of Education, Dorothy Gardner (1969). In particular, he presents a more thorough assessment of Issacs' crucial role in the quarrels that rent the British Psychoanalytic Society and occupied the forefront of her attention in her last years (she died of cancer in 1948 at the age of 63).

Background

Grace is a five-year-old girl, the eldest daughter in an intact white middle-class family. She is bilingual, as her mother is Northern European. Grace's father is a self-employed professional and her mother works part time. Because of complications in the pregnancy, Grace was born a month early and was very underweight. At this time, Grace's mother was largely unsupported by Grace's father because of his work commitments. Initially Grace was tube fed, and her mother later struggled to breastfeed her. Grace was then bottle-fed; however, this too proved problematic, with Grace often vomiting after a feed. She was hard to settle at night and apparently only slept through the night around the age of two years. Her other milestones appear to have been normal, and in fact she was described as being quite forward in some, such as walking and talking. I had the impression that Grace's mother found it difficult to acknowledge quite what a vulnerable baby Grace had been, and delighted in what she saw as Grace's superior intellect. Grace refused to use a potty to defecate and the difficulties appear to have worsened around the time her sister was born, two years ago. Grace was increasingly troubled with constipation and was referred to the paediatric service at the age of three. Laxatives and enemas were prescribed and for about 18 months, the family were offered advice and behavioural management. However, Grace steadfastly refused to use the toilet. She was eventually referred to her local CAMHS service at four and a half.

When I assessed the family, Grace's parents were very keen to impress upon me that they viewed her constipation as a symptom of a wider problem. They described their daughter as anxious and always expecting the worst in new situations. This description was in stark contrast to that of their sociable and robust second child. They also described Grace as being extremely sensitive to light and noise. She found playtimes at school especially difficult and found it difficult to make friendships and join in with her peers. Grace's parents welcomed the opportunity to think about her emotional experience, and have continued to be very receptive to the help that has been offered. I undertook an individual assessment of Grace and following this began to see her for psychoanalytic psychotherapy on an intensive basis. Alongside this, a colleague has been seeing Grace's parents on a less intensive basis. During the initial few months of the therapy, Grace was often silent or spoke only in whispers. For much of the time she was hidden in corners of the room or under the blanket. Often, the sessions appeared more like infant observations, with only fragments of play discernible.

Author biographies

Teresa Bailey is Head of Child Psychotherapy in a South London CAMHS Service. She is a member of the BAP Training Committee and is Assistant Editor of the Journal. She has a particular interest in depression and trauma in adolescents. She previously worked for many years in the South London and Maudsley Trust and has also worked at Open Door, Young People's Consultation Service.

Susanna Billström is a licensed psychologist at a community-based unit within the department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Stockholm County Council, Sweden. She is also a trained child psychotherapist at the Erica Foundation, Stockholm, where she also contributes to research in child psychotherapy. She has a special research interest in child interviewing.

Belinda Blecher is a child and adolescent psychotherapist who works both in Sydney Children's Hospital with under fives and also at the Royal Hospital for Women where she works on the neo-natal unit with mothers and babies. She also works in private practice and runs a small consultancy business that supports preschools in the eastern suburbs of Sydney.

Ornella Caccia is a child psychotherapist, qualified at the Tavistock Clinic in 1982. She lives and works in Rome (Italy). She is a teacher and a supervisor in the courses for child psychotherapists held in Rome by the AIPPI (Italian Association for Child Psychotherapists) and in Florence by the Centro Studi Matha Harris. She works in conjunction with the Tavistock Clinic and the University of East London as academic tutor for courses in observational studies. She has contributed to the Journal of Child Psychotherapy, to the Journal of Infant Observation and to several books and journals edited in Italy.

Gunnar Carlberg, PhD, is an Associate Professor at the University of Stockholm and Director of the Erica Foundation in Stockholm, an institute providing psychotherapy for children and adolescents, professional training at university level, and research. He is a licensed psychologist and psychotherapist with numerous publications on psychodynamic developmental psychology and child psychotherapy research. One of his main interests is ‘turning points’ in child psychotherapy. Furthermore, he is project-leader of the Erica Process and Outcome Study (EPOS).

Editorial

Viviane Green and Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley  

This volume of the JCP has two mini-themes: work with autistic children and research findings linked to clinical practice. ‘The Sound-Hand’ by Francesco Bisagni, is a highly original contribution to understanding the ‘mindscape’ of an autistic boy through therapeutic communication initially with ‘sounds’ and the child's drawing of a hand. The sound-hand, the author suggests, offers a way of thinking about how a mind emerges. The article integrates understanding based on Jung, Bion, neuroscience and chaos theory to give an account of the growth of subjectivity and the emergent mind. Refreshingly, the author explores how he allows himself to use his countertransference to understand his patient without recourse to therapeutic cliches, ‘the language of despair’.

Careful attention to countertranserference is also a feature of the article by Vera Regina Fonseca. In the ‘The autistic dialogic style: a case of Asperger's syndrome’, she describes intensive work with Arthur, a 12-year-old boy who has the tendency to induce drowsiness in the analyst, a phenomenon that many, perhaps, will recognise. Building on her earlier work, Fonseca considers the restriction of dialogic style, and the reduction of the analytic encounter to rigid question-and-answer sessions by her patient in an effort to avoid an experience of ‘otherness’. This is gradually overcome as life, liveliness and symbolic activity are kindled.

Kleinschmidt's article about psychotherapy with a traumatised teenager and her infant daughter, following trafficking to the UK from Eastern Europe after a period of detention, abuse and forced prostitution, is a moving account of a patient working through traumatic events and in doing so, painfully recognises the separate existence of her daughter. Intergenerational issues are of particular interest in this article, as the writer strives to frame the emotional transactions between mother and daughter. Another striking aspect of the article is the exploration of some of the difficulties of working with an interpreter, not least the emotional impact on the interpreter, and the implicit challenges of cross-cultural work.

Editorial

This is a special themed issue on Gender Identity. It brings together a collection of papers from the ACP 2008 Annual Conference, with a guest contribution by Dr Domenico Di Ceglie on gender identity disorder (GID) entitled ‘Engaging young people with atypical gender identity development in therapeutic work: a developmental approach’. Di Ceglie's specialist experience in offering a GID service offers a broad overview and he highlights some of the service management issues. He puts forward the view that when working with the children and families of GID, focusing on keeping the developmental process open is more productive than only focusing on the GID itself. An assessment period reveals the degree to which the desire to belong to the opposite gender is a wish or a powerful belief with important consequences for outcome and whether or not gender reassignment is pursued.

Jenny Sprince's illuminating article, ‘The devil and the deep blue sea: dyadic narcissism and the problem of individuation,’ explores issues of infantile gender identifications with a specific focus on ‘gender narcissism’ and the impact this can have on bisexual and triadic functioning. Sprince draws on her in-depth understanding of group processes amongst adolescents and their carers, gained through her therapeutic and consultation work in institutional settings, and she illustrates her themes with material from this work. She discusses the ideas of ‘dyadic narcissism’ and ‘phallic narcissism’, how these are linked to particular constructions of ‘feminine’ and ‘masculine’, and how these in turn are linked to sado-masochism.

The next article is ‘Exposed: phallic protections, shame and damaged parental objects’, by Simon Cregeen. Cregeen discusses the ‘phallic state of mind’, which may be turned to as a form of psychic survival in the face of catastrophic experience and anxieties. This article links particularly well with the previous one in its exploration of ‘phallic narcissism’, and indeed both authors make reference to and draw on Birksted-Breen's (1996) important article ‘Phallus, penis and mental space’ (International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, 77: 649–57). Cregeen compellingly uses graphic and thought-provoking clinical material from his individual therapeutic work with boys to elucidate his ideas, including an extended case history. He explores the experience of shame and the way in which it is connected with damaged and damaging internal objects. Cregeen's article demonstrates how in some cases the countertransference experience of the therapist may be a central and critical source of understanding.

Anthony Lee is a child and adolescent psychotherapist with a particular interest in work with children and young people with endocrine difficulties. He also works as part of the Autism Service at the Tavistock Clinic, London. He was formerly member of the Developmental Psychopathology Research Unit (DPRU), Tavistock Clinic, London.

Charlotte Jarvis is a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist who from 1998–2007 was the director of Open Door, Young People's Consultation Service, a voluntary sector service based in north London for young people (aged 12–24) and the parents of young people (12–21). Editorial

Viviane Green and Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley  

This issue of the Journal contains a wide range of papers on theoretical, clinical and research topics.

Caccia's article explores the theoretical landscape of primal splitting with an erudite and in-depth consideration of the development of Kleinian thought, including the key influences of Meltzer and Bion. She considers defects in early splitting processes and their impact on cognitive and emotional development by means of a detailed case study. Sensitive clinical work is described with three-year-old Roberto, who was referred with extreme feeding problems and separation issues that greatly improve over the course of his psychotherapy. Of particular interest in the article is how Caccia modifies her technique actively to address particular distortions of truth and perception while simultaneously holding and working with Roberto in the transference relationship.

Issues pertaining to technique are also in evidence in the first of two papers by Swedish authors. May Nilsson's centres on the use of games in psychotherapy with children, and their potential meaning and benefit. The view that games are therapeutically useful is a theme often echoed in recent papers published in the JCP. Nilsson vividly describes her twice-weekly psychotherapy with Peter, a four-and-a-half-year-old autistic boy who inadvertently discovers a game of table hockey in the consulting room, a situation that will undoubtedly resonate with many readers who have experienced similar, unexpected occurrences in the course of clinical work. In Peter's case, his discovery becomes a pivotal point in his treatment as his psychotherapist skilfully incorporates the use of the game during sessions, in an active approach to reach him.

The theme of emotional growth and the difficulties inherent therein, are the subject of Music and Chantrell's papers and interestingly, echoed in the theme of emotional readiness in the clinical commentary.

In ‘Neglecting neglect’, Music makes an original contribution to furthering our understanding of working with children who, whilst they may not have suffered the worst extremes of abuse, have been stultified in the growth of their emotional capacities through the cumulative effects of emotional neglect. Clinicians will recognise the child's inner ‘deadness’ induced by countertransference responses of frustration and boredom. Clinical examples are set in the context of a broader neuroscientific understanding of what it means to the individual child's development when live, emotionally attuned company has been denied. Emotional growth is also explored in Chantrell's paper on her once-weekly work with an eight-year-old learning-disabled girl. Her paper looks at how a learning disability impacts on emotional growth and her patient Ellie's capacity to manage her inner self or ‘reality ego’. Through Chantrell's careful observation and painstaking work, Ellie's kicks, bites and hair pulling are gradually replaced by words and her capacity to learn develops.

Primal splitting as a basis for emotional and cognitive development in children

Ornella Caccia

Ornella Caccia

Ornella Caccia  

primal splitting, combined object, cognitive development, intergenerational transmission

This article discusses the importance of good primal splitting as the basis for the child's emotional and cognitive development. A theoretical introduction analyses the possible pathologies of primal splitting, as they were first pointed out by Melanie Klein and then by some post-Kleinian authors, in particular Donald Meltzer. This is followed by some excerpts from the clinical material of the first year of the psychoanalytic psychotherapy of a three-year-old child suffering from eating problems. Starting from the child's play activity, the author tries to identify the splitting problems that underlie the child's view of the world, and to address these with him. The article shows how at times it can be useful to speak also to the child's intelligence, combining the usual analytic work (containment of anxiety and analysis of transference) with the analysis of the child's distortions and cognitive misconceptions. The article also suggests that faulty primal splitting tends to be transmitted from one generation to the next.

Effectiveness of child psychoanalytic psychotherapy in a clinical outpatient setting

Elisabeth Deakin and Maria Tiellet Nunes

Maria Tiellet Nunes

Maria Tiellet Nunes  

Child, psychotherapy, outcome, psychoanalysis, psychological evaluation, effectiveness

The objective of this study was to evaluate the outcome of child psychoanalytic psychotherapy in a clinical outpatient setting in a city in southern Brazil. Three psychological tests (Rorschach, Bender and WISC III) were administered to 23 children, aged 6–11 years old, and the Child Behaviour Check List (CBCL) was completed by the parents. All testing was completed before the beginning of the individual psychoanalytic psychotherapy. The same measures were repeated after 12 months of intervention. The 23 children who received individual psychoanalytic psychotherapy were compared with a control group who did not receive any kind of intervention. In the clinical group, the results indicated a statistically significant reduction of anxiety symptoms (0.002) and school problems (0.031), improvement in interpersonal relationships (0.022), and positive change in the following CBCL scales: withdrawn (0.010), thought problems (0.022), anxiety and depression (0.017), internalising (0.008) and total (0.003). An effect size of 0.696 was calculated based on the CBCL total scale before and after the intervention. The results revealed that child psychoanalytical psychotherapy is mostly effective in the treatment of female children who present internalising disorders.

To make a male: what does it take?1

Jane Elfer and Anthony Lee

Anthony Lee

Anthony Lee  

hospital work, parent and child work, gender identity, internal working couple, secondary handicap

This article presents a case study of a year of psychotherapeutic work by a female and male therapist with a 14-year-old boy born with ambiguous genitalia. His mother was also present in the sessions at the request of Zak. We describe the early trauma surrounding Zak's birth and the subsequent desertion of a violent father. We present the catalogue of medical interventions he received to re-construct his genitals. Now at the age of 14 years Zak is entering into a chemically induced puberty. His mother had a version of an internal couple at war, where the male was viewed as useless and with suspicion. This view served to distort her capacity to bear Zak's condition and dovetailed with his phantasy of a monstrously violent and destructive male. Thus the artificial shove into manhood for Zak was filled with terror. The induced puberty was felt more like an attack and he acted out through resistance to intervention and non-compliance. This organisation created in him a state of thoughtlessness and despair, which we propose parades itself as a ‘secondary handicap’ (Sinason, Mental Handicap and the Human Condition, Free Association, London, 1992). Our joint work as a couple with Zak and his mother stood in opposition to their internal structures and provided an experience of a different kind of coupling: an opportunity to observe a cooperatively working couple who helped give words to the anxieties they brought. We trace Zak's attachment to and internalisation of a thinking couple, which paralleled both his ability to become more expressive and a reduction in acting out his aggression. The work aimed to promote in Zak a level of emotional development that was commensurate with his physical development. The construction of genitals and a lifetime of testosterone injections alone will not allow Zak to grow into the man he can be. We will attempt to explore the basis of these structures to demonstrate that the work provided the opportunity for Zak to reflect upon and express his terror, and to turn to other people to seek support, help and advice.

Lyndall Kleinschmidt

Lyndall Kleinschmidt  

Psychoanalytic psychotherapy, projective identification, mother–infant, dead mother, PTSD

The power of new traumatic events to reignite memories and the distress of traumatic experiences earlier in life is well known to psychotherapists. When the recent trauma has been extreme, the task of assisting the patient to understand their response in the light of their earlier experience can be doubly challenging. This paper describes the therapy with an adolescent girl and her infant daughter, following the girl's escape from illegal detention, physical abuse and forced prostitution, after she was trafficked to the UK from Eastern Europe. The discussion works towards developing an understanding of the emotional interchange between the mother and infant, and the influence of the mother's traumatic experiences, on that interchange. Projective identification could be seen to occur from the mother, into her daughter, in a reversal of the situation traditionally described. The function of this for the mother and the impact on the developing infant, are considered.

Growth in emotional intelligence. Psychotherapy with a learning disabled girl

Sue Chantrell

Sue Chantrell

Sue Chantrell  

emotional intelligence, learning disability, inner world, containment, reality ego, depressive position, trauma, limitations

This paper describes the once-weekly psychoanalytic psychotherapy of a girl, called Ellie, aged eight at the start of her treatment. Ellie had a learning disability and displayed difficult behaviour at school and at home. In her therapy, Ellie grew in emotional intelligence, more in touch with and able to express her feelings. Her behaviour improved and so did her capacity to learn. In the therapy there were certain limitations to progress and this is discussed in terms of how Ellie's disability affected the basic achievements of emotional development, including a mind with a solid ‘reality ego’, able to contain anxiety, and able to maintain depressive functioning. The importance of parallel parent work, to share observations and understanding of the child's functioning is discussed. Difficulties for both child and parents in dealing with the pain of difference and how this limits emotional intelligence are discussed. The author hopes that this paper will encourage the offering of psychoanalytic psychotherapy to children and young people with learning disabilities, who are significantly more likely to suffer from mental health problems than their peers.

[[RunningHead]]

The autistic dialogic style: a case of Asperger's syndrome

Vera Regina Fonseca

Vera Regina Fonseca

Vera Regina Fonseca  

Autistic disorders, developmental psychopathology, dialogism, Asperger's syndrome

In a former study (Fonseca and Bussab, 2006, ‘Self, other and dialogical space in autistic states’, International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, 87:1–16), the author hypothesised that in autistic disorders there is a distortion in the construction of what she defined as dialogic space. Such a space, in which self and other define each other mutually, is the final result of early dyadic transactions. These are characterised by opposing experiences of ongoing regulation, disruption and repair. This sets the basis for both the sense of predictability, the so-called ‘me experiences’, in Winnicottian terminology, and novelty, the ‘not-me experiences’. The balance of these transactions provides the preconditions for the acceptance of otherness, a crucial difficulty in autistic disorders, whose hallmark is considered by some authors to be the inability to accept and deal with otherness. This paper aims to illustrate the peculiar way in which such difficulties are made clear in less severe cases on the autistic spectrum, such as in Asperger's syndrome. The clinical material of a 12-year-old-boy with an uncanny ability to induce drowsiness in the analyst will be presented. My hypothesis is that such a state is the consequence of a dialogic style of forcing agreement inside the dyad, searching exclusively for the already known, as a possible way of avoiding the encounter with otherness.

Children's expectations and experiences of psychodynamic child psychotherapy

Gunnar Carlberg , Agneta Thorén , Susanna Billström and Fredrik Odhammar

Fredrik Odhammar

Fredrik Odhammar  

interview, child's testimony, narrative, clinically based study, qualitative research, therapeutic alliance

The aim of this study was to explore children's expectations and experiences of psychodynamic child psychotherapy. Semi-structured interviews were conducted using self-rating instruments, drawing materials and a selection of toys. Ten children aged 6–10 years were interviewed prior to and after treatment (mean number of sessions = 99). The main results showed that most of the children, despite their young age, had the ability to give clinically valuable accounts, verbally or non-verbally, of their problems. A majority of the children expressed positive hopes and expectations about their forthcoming therapy as well as regarding the experience of therapy as positive or very positive after termination. Self-ratings of change showed a moderate degree of improvement in their problems. Pre-treatment attitudes were linked with post-treatment self-ratings of improvement. The importance of preparing the child and the family for therapy and of listening to the children's experiences is highlighted.

[[RunningHead]]

Clinical Commentary

Clinical material

Background

Sarah is a white British adolescent who lives with her mother and father in a small town in the north of England. She was referred by her GP to the local Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service at the age of 17 following the breakdown of a relationship with a boyfriend. After discovering that intimate and humiliating details of their sexual contact had been shared with several of her friends, Sarah had refused to return to college and had started cutting her arms and legs – causing superficial scratches – with a razor blade. Over time, I learned that her mother had responded to Sarah's self-harming by moving her daughter into the parental bed; her father, I was told, slept in the living room during this period. Shortly after the referral, her mother secured Sarah a job as a waitress in the local restaurant where she worked as manager. Sarah has three older brothers, all living away from home. The referral reported that mother had a stress-related illness, which had resulted in several hospitalisations during Sarah's infancy. Sarah, too, suffered from regular bouts of irritable bowel syndrome.

Following an assessment with another clinician, Sarah began once-weekly psychotherapy. My first impressions were of an attractive, provocatively dressed girl – with tattoos and body piercings – who would spend long stretches of her early sessions in silence, tapping her teeth with her tongue stud or carefully picking at her clothing. Her wish seemed to be to make me curious and closely attentive to her body, while maintaining a distance between us. Slowly, however, Sarah began to talk, going on to describe the ways in which her mother would remove knives and other sharp instruments from the house in an attempt to prevent her from harming herself. With considerable satisfaction she would insist that her mother's actions made no difference – she could always, she told me, find other ways of cutting. Her father – who worked as a lorry driver – was rarely mentioned.

This commentary looks at two sessions with a five-year-old girl called Grace. In these extracts from her intensive psychotherapy, we see a move from isolation, impoverished interaction and silence or whispers (interesting in a child who is bilingual) to symbolic communicative play and verbal interactions with the therapist. What accounts for this shift? The therapist is clear that there were no obvious precipitating causes for this increased communicativeness.

[[RunningHead]]

Engaging young people with atypical gender identity development in therapeutic work: a developmental approach

Domenico Di Ceglie

Domenico Di Ceglie

Domenico Di Ceglie  

gender identity disorder (GID), atypical gender identity development, developmental approach, therapeutic aims for GID, persistence and desistence of GID

Gender identity disorders (GID) in young people are complex and often distressing conditions. The paper starts by examining the experience of the professional worker resulting from the interaction with this group of young people and their families. This is frequently characterised by a sense of being under pressure and in danger. The view put forward is that the position of professionals often mirrors the mental state of these young people, which is described by the metaphor ‘working at the edge’. The issue of how to move to a position of safety for the young person and the professional is addressed. The paper describes a developmental model of care based on psychodynamic understanding, and distinguishes between conditions that are transient and conditions that persist during the course of development. Possible factors involved in the persistence of the ‘atypical gender identity organisation’ are considered based on Baron-Cohen's concepts of systemising and empathising. The therapeutic aims in working with these young people are revisited 10 years on from the first publication. Two contrasting cases are used to illustrate the persistence or desistence of the GID in the course of development. The paper concludes that while there is a tendency to move to provide hormonal interventions early for adolescents who are considered not amenable to change in their atypical gender identity, the integration of psychological, social and, when appropriate, hormonal interventions remains central to the provision of good standards of care.

Exposed: phallic protections, shame and damaged parental objects1

Simon Cregeen

Simon Cregeen

Simon Cregeen  

phallic functioning, psychic bisexuality, internal couple, shame, penis-as-link, trauma

Using ideas derived from Dana Birksted-Breen (‘Phallus, penis and mental space’, International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, 77: 649–57, 1996), this article explores the clinical experience with ‘Tommy’, a young boy who suffered multiple traumas and neglect. Birksted-Breen describes a phallic state of mind, which, amongst other things, serves to repudiate the potential for a creative link between internal parental objects and a capacity for thinking. In order to survive psychically, Tommy frequently turned to a phallic state of mind. The deficits in his internal and external objects meant that helpful parental qualities, linked with the development of psychic bisexuality, were not available for introjection and identification. The paper suggests a link between Tommy's employment of phallic (and at times perverse) ways of thinking, related to his intrusive attempts to expose and humiliate his psychotherapist, and to an experience of shame associated with inadequate internal objects. The serious compromise to the development of a creative psychic bisexuality in the patient is reflected in the countertransference strain on the psychotherapist's own internal couple.

[[RunningHead]]

Neglecting neglect: some thoughts about children who have lacked good input, and are ‘undrawn’ and ‘unenjoyed’

Graham Music

Graham Music

Graham Music  

emotional, neglect, undrawn, deprivation, neuroscience, avoidant, attachment, regulation, pleasure, neglected children

This paper looks at emotional neglect in the early years of life, and postulates some probable long-term sequelae of such neglect. It argues that there is a continuum of neglect; ranging from the severest form, as seen in institutional orphanages, to milder variations. A range of theoretical and research traditions, including developmental psychology, attachment theory and neuroscience are used, alongside psychoanalytic ideas, to attempt to delineate some of the key features and patterns that arise. A question is raised as to whether we have sufficient diagnostic categories or theoretical ideas to make sense of neglected children. Thought is given to the very specific clinical challenges of working with children who are neglected, and how the clinical task might differ from working with children who have suffered other forms of early damage, such as physical abuse. It is argued that these children suffer a multiple, overdetermined form of neglect; their initial neglect because of the form of caretaking they did (or did not) receive being compounded by their inability to use help and then also the tendency of professionals to similarly neglect these children, who can be difficult to relate to and hard to ‘warm’ to.

[[RunningHead]]

The sound-hand

Francesco Bisagni

Francesco Bisagni

Francesco Bisagni  

Autism, rhythm, emergent mind, analyst's subjectivity

Through clinical vignettes taken from the analytic treatment of an autistic child, the paper explores Bion' s notion of selected fact in relation to the post-Jungian theoretical speculation on the emergent mind. The issue of the subjectivity of the analyst is considered and explored in this light. A review of some neuroscience research contributions to a possible understanding of dialogue, empathy and rhythm is briefly described, particularly in terms of its potential usefulness for the psychoanalytic mind when working with autistic children. In general, the notions of ‘temporal shapes’ (Alvarez) and ‘sound-object’ (Maiello) provide support for the theoretical and clinical explorations of the issue of rhythmic interactions. Rhythmic sounds are distinguished from stereotypical and meaningless sounds produced by the analysand, whether or not they are accompanied by body movements, and their function of activating representations and amplifications in the analyst's mind is explored in the stage of treatment when the child does not yet speak. The Jungian concept of amplification is considered and revisited in this context.

[[RunningHead]]

What can the matter be?

Hazel Douglas

Hazel Douglas

Hazel Douglas  

What can the matter be?, edited by Louise Emanuel with Elizabeth Bradley, London, Karnac, 2008, 294 pp., £18.99

What can the Matter be? Therapeutic Interventions with Parents, Infants and Young Children, is part of the Tavistock Clinic Series and showcases the work of the Tavistock Clinic's Under Fives Service.

The Foreword by Margaret Rustin gives an interesting historical perspective, as she chronicles the origins of the service in the 1970s, arising from her ideas about how to encourage families with babies and young children to access help. The emphasis in the academic literature at that time would have been on individual work with the child, so this thinking represented a shift towards applying ideas from child psychotherapy to the family rather than mainly focussing on the internal world of the child and towards applying the work within a brief therapy model. The book shows how successful this leap in practice has proved to be through the work and ideas of the contributors to this book: Paul Barrows, Elizabeth Bradley, Dilys Daws, Louise Emanuel, Michi Gurion, Juliet Hopkins, Meira Likierman, Lisa Miller, Janine Sternberg, Beverley Tydeman, Cathy Urwin and Isca Wittenberg.

The Introduction outlines the work of the clinic, summarising the theoretical framework and describing the intervention. The theory emphasises the importance of Bion's concept of containment, but in practice also integrates psychoanalytical concepts with other ideas.

An understanding of attachment theory, child development, and neurosciences research offers multiple perspectives to the work, and ideas stemming from systemic family therapy may also contribute to clinical practice with under fives. (p. 3)

The astonishing aspect of this brief intervention is the rapidity of change that can occur when working with the whole system at once. This doesn't happen all the time and sometimes children and parents will need to move into other therapies, but it is amazing that such productive change can happen in such a short time. This is of especial clinical significance because changing the life trajectory of a child at such a young age has potentially more impact than change which occurs later, if we take into account findings from neuroscience and child development research.
